title: Anselm's argument
hook: God is that than which nothing greater can be thought

segments.voice: Yesterday, John of Damascus and the icons: the maker of matter became matter. Your line was matter is not evil.

A monk is stuck. By his own account, he's been hunting for one single argument, short and complete, that would show God exists. It keeps slipping away. He tries to give up on it, and it won't leave him alone. Then one day it arrives, and he writes it down. His name is Anselm, and the surprise is where he puts the argument. Not in a lecture. In a prayer. The little book opens with Anselm talking to God, asking to see God's face. Only then, mid-prayer, does he make his move.

First, his reason for arguing at all. In words close to his: I don't seek to understand so that I can believe. I believe so that I can understand. Faith, looking for understanding. Then he turns to a psalm: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God." He starts with a definition. God is something than which nothing greater can be thought. Even the fool understands those words, so the idea is at least in his mind. Now a painter. Before painting, the picture is in the painter's mind. After, it's in the mind and on the wall. Which is greater? The one that's real too. So if that-than-which-nothing-greater-can-be-thought existed only in the mind, you could think of something greater: the same thing, but real. And that can't be. So, Anselm concludes, it must exist in reality. Not everyone was convinced. A monk named Gaunilo wrote a reply on behalf of the fool: picture an island more perfect than any other; does that make it real? Anselm answered him, and the debate is still going among philosophers. But a few chapters later comes one more turn, the source of today's line. God, Anselm says, is not only that than which nothing greater can be thought. God is greater than can be thought. For Anselm, the argument isn't a fence around God. It ends at an edge, with more past it than the mind can hold.

Let your mind reach for the biggest, best thing it can hold: mountains, oceans, a love that never fails, the whole night sky. Notice that whatever you've got, you can still think of something greater, and rest there, at the edge of your thinking. If you pray, you can turn toward God the way Anselm did, talking first.
Anselm's argument. God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, and, Anselm adds, greater than can be thought at all, an argument made inside a prayer.
Your line: greater than can be thought. For Anselm, the edge of thinking was a place to pray. That's today, done.

howItsDone: Christians meet Anselm's argument in philosophy and theology classes, where it is still argued for and against; some also read his Proslogion as a book of prayer.

fork.reveal: Anselm wrote a reply to Gaunilo and kept his argument. the debate is still going among philosophers.

what it means: Anselm's argument begins in prayer: if God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, God can't exist only in the mind.
what a scholar hears: Proslogion 15, where the definition flips: God is greater than can be thought, so the argument opens onto mystery.

chat.says: Can you really prove God exists just by thinking about it?
options: Anselm tried, inside a prayer, from God as that than which nothing greater can be thought.
Anselm said yes, and everyone agreed at once; no one has ever objected to it.
Anselm said no; he thought faith and thinking had nothing to do with each other.
chat.meaning: Anselm argued, inside a prayer, from God as that than which nothing greater can be thought. Gaunilo objected, and philosophers still debate it.

notes: Anselm is paraphrased throughout (Deane's 1903 translation is not on the validator's list). Check: the search for a single argument (preface); the opening prayer and 'I believe in order to understand' (ch. 1); the definition, the fool, and the painter (ch. 2); 'greater than can be thought' (ch. 15).
The hook paraphrases the preface (he sought a single argument, nearly gave up, and the thought would not leave him); confirm.
'The debate is still going among philosophers' is general; confirm acceptable.
'Faith seeking understanding' was Anselm's original title for the Proslogion (Fides quaerens intellectum); not stated in the script, only used as a screen head.

Editor pass: the teach's last line now frames the claim as Anselm's ('For Anselm, ...') rather than the narrator's, and trades the door image (day 1232's theme) for the edge image the carry uses. Gaunilo's island rephrased closer to his 'more excellent than all other lands'.
Original: 'aliquid quo nihil maius cogitari possit' from Proslogion 2; ecclesiastical pronunciation would differ (MAH-yoos, koh-jee-TAH-ree).
